founders: Vishrant Dave, Prateesh Awasthi, Ayush Ranjan
tech: Snake-like, hyper-redundant robotic arms that inspect confined industrial spaces
problem: People still crawl into fuel tanks, ship hulls and jet engines for inspections, which is slow and dangerous
eli12: Imagine a robot arm that bends like a snake, with more than 20 joints, so it can wriggle through a gap narrower than a soda can and look around inside a tank. Today a person has to climb in. The hard part is controlling that many joints at once without the arm crashing into walls, which is where the AI navigation comes in.
signal: $2.1M pre-seed led by pi Ventures; reported in talks for a much larger round; targets 10–12 pilots
why: Confined-space inspection is a safety problem with a regulatory forcing function; a platform arm can sell into aviation, oil and gas, shipbuilding and nuclear without a rebuild.

founders: CoinDCX co-founder with ex-ISRO scientists (names not in source)
tech: Full-flow staged-combustion methane-oxygen rocket engine for medium-lift launch
problem: India needs reusable, high-thrust engines to compete on launch cost
eli12: A rocket engine burns fuel and oxygen to push the rocket up. This design pre-burns both before the main chamber, which squeezes more push out of every kilo of fuel and is gentler on the parts, so the engine can fly again. Only SpaceX has flown this kind of engine. It's very hard because the pumps and pipes run hot and at crushing pressure.
signal: Selected for IN-SPACe Technology Adoption Fund support
funding: ~$7M early round (2025) plus IN-SPACe TAF award
why: A government grant on top of private money is a co-signal that the hardest engine cycle is being taken seriously; reusability is the cost lever in launch.

tech: In-orbit computing for satellites, plus an AI-powered star tracker
problem: Satellites send raw data down for processing, which is slow and bandwidth-hungry
eli12: Satellites take huge pictures but have to beam them all down to Earth before anyone can use them, like mailing every photo you take to a lab. TakeMe2Space puts a small computer on the satellite so it can do the work up there and send only the answer. Its star tracker works like a sailor using stars to know which way the ship is pointing.
signal: Selected for IN-SPACe Technology Adoption Fund (AI star tracker)
funding: ₹5.5 Cr pre-seed (2025), Seafund; IN-SPACe TAF award
why: Edge compute in orbit is a picks-and-shovels play on India's satellite boom; the government grant is a second, independent vote.

tech: In-orbit servicing to extend the life of geostationary satellites
problem: Big satellites retire when fuel runs out even if everything else works
eli12: Big communication satellites sit very far from Earth and get thrown away when their fuel tank is empty, even if the rest works fine. It's like scrapping a car because it ran out of petrol. Aule is building a servicer that flies up, docks, and keeps them going. The hard part is grabbing a fast-moving satellite safely.
signal: $2M pre-seed led by pi Ventures; earlier IN-SPACe seed support; defence interest
why: Life-extension is a service with a clear buyer (satellite operators) and a dual-use defence angle in space situational awareness.

tech: Multi-mission navigation-and-communication satellite constellation
problem: Strategic dependence on foreign navigation and comms satellites
eli12: Your phone's map uses signals from satellites to know where you are. Most of those belong to other countries. Sanyark wants to build a group of satellites that do both navigation and communication for India. It's hard because you need many satellites working together before it's useful at all.
signal: $500K pre-seed from AUM Ventures
why: A sovereignty bet that needs many satellites before revenue; capital intensity is the first diligence question.

tech: ATOM satellite thruster and CUBEHOOD demo mission
problem: Small satellites need compact, reliable propulsion to move and stay in orbit
eli12: A small satellite drifts unless it can nudge itself, like a boat needing a small engine. Dream Aerospace makes tiny thrusters for that. Its next step is to test the thruster to space standards and fly a demo.
signal: ₹10 Cr pre-Series A for thruster qualification and a demo mission
why: Propulsion is a component every small satellite needs; qualification data will decide whether this is a supplier or a science project.

tech: AI systems that automate custom chip design
problem: Designing a chip takes large expert teams and many months
eli12: Designing a computer chip is like planning a city with billions of tiny roads that must never cross wrong. Engineers spend months on it. Tattvam teaches AI to do big parts of that planning automatically. The hard part is that one tiny mistake ruins a very expensive manufacturing run.
signal: $1.7M pre-seed led by Seedcamp
why: Chip-design labour is the bottleneck for India's fabless ambitions; tooling sells to every chip team rather than betting on one chip.

tech: Analog in-memory compute chips with optical interconnects for AI
problem: AI chips waste most of their energy shuttling data between memory and processor
eli12: Normal chips keep moving numbers back and forth between a 'storage room' and a 'thinking room', and that walking burns most of the power. optoML does the maths right inside the storage room and uses light instead of wires to move data between chips. The hard part: analog maths is noisy, so it has to stay accurate.
signal: $1.8M pre-Series A led by Bluehill.VC and a99
why: AI energy cost is the industry's binding constraint; in-memory plus optical is a genuinely different architecture, not a cheaper copy.

tech: Ultra-low-power edge-AI chips combining compute, connectivity and sensing
problem: IoT, automotive and medical devices need small chips that think locally on tiny batteries
eli12: Smart devices like fitness bands or sensors need a tiny brain that runs on almost no battery. Sensesemi packs the brain, the radio and the senses onto one small chip. The hard part is doing all three while sipping power.
signal: ₹25 Cr seed led by Piper Serica to fund tape-outs in 2026
why: Government DLI approval de-risks part of the design cost; the test is first silicon and an OEM design win.

tech: Fabless system-on-chip design; first commercial chip taped out
problem: India imports nearly all the chips in its devices
eli12: A system-on-chip is a whole computer squeezed onto one chip, like the brain inside a CCTV camera or a smart meter. BigEndian designs them in India and has already sent its first design to the factory. The hard part is winning customers who are used to buying proven foreign chips.
signal: $6M pre-Series A led by IAN Alpha Fund with Vertex and IvyCap
funding: $6M pre-Series A, IAN Alpha, Vertex, IvyCap
why: A completed tape-out moves the risk from 'can they build it' to 'can they sell it', which is the right risk to underwrite at this stage.

tech: AI-led chemical R&D and production for speciality chemicals and pharma
problem: Process chemistry for drug ingredients is slow, trial-and-error and often imported
eli12: Making a medicine ingredient is like following a very long, fussy recipe. NuSynth uses AI to find better recipes faster, testing fewer batches before one works cheaply and safely. The hard part: a recipe that works in a beaker often fails in a giant factory tank.
signal: ₹36.5 Cr seed co-led by Avaana Capital and Shastra VC
funding: ₹36.5 Cr seed, Avaana Capital & Shastra VC
why: India manufactures the world's generics but rents much of the process know-how; owning the recipe is the higher-margin layer.

tech: India-built direct-drive linear motion systems for industrial automation
problem: Precision linear motors for machines and robots are largely imported
eli12: Many factory machines need parts that slide back and forth very precisely, like a super-accurate drawer. Usually gears and belts do this and they wear out. Quintrans uses magnets to push the part directly, with no gears, and builds it in India. The hard part is precision at a price Indian factories will pay.
signal: $750K pre-seed led by Capital-A; IIMA Ventures an existing backer
why: An unglamorous import-substitution component that every automation OEM buys; distribution, not science, is the risk.

tech: India-built service robotics
problem: Service robots for commercial spaces are mostly imported
eli12: Service robots are the ones that guide visitors, carry things or clean in places like hospitals and malls. Alphadroid builds them in India. The hard part is making them reliable around crowds of people every day.
signal: $3.8M pre-Series A (categorised as seed)
why: Domestic service robotics is a cost play against imports; worth checking deployments and unit economics before the technology.

tech: Hydrogen-ready micro gas turbines for clean power, mobility and aerospace
problem: Backup and off-grid power still runs mostly on diesel
eli12: A gas turbine is like a jet engine bolted to the ground, spinning to make electricity. Hycosys makes small ones that can run on hydrogen, which leaves water instead of smoke. The hard part: hydrogen burns very hot and fast, so the turbine has to handle it without melting or knocking.
signal: Over $1M seed led by MountTech Growth Fund – Kavachh
why: Fuel-flexible turbines hedge the hydrogen bet: they sell on today's fuels and upgrade as hydrogen gets cheaper.

tech: Iron-air long-duration batteries (16–24 hours)
problem: Lithium batteries are too expensive for storing solar power through the night
eli12: Solar panels make power by day, but we need it at night too. Lithium batteries are great for a few hours but too pricey for a whole night. Meine's battery basically lets iron rust and un-rust, storing energy cheaply for a full day. The hard part is making it charge fast and last many years.
signal: $750K pre-seed from Antler, Rebalance, Venture Catalysts and others; moving from lab prototypes to pilot systems
why: Iron is cheap and Indian; if the chemistry holds, long-duration storage is the missing piece of a solar-heavy grid.

tech: Next-generation battery cells for Indian conditions, with pilot-scale manufacturing
problem: Imported cells struggle with heat, fast charging and safety in Indian use
eli12: Battery cells are the little cans inside an EV battery pack. Most are imported and designed for cooler countries. e-TRNL designs cells that charge fast and stay safe in Indian heat, and is starting to make them. The hard part is manufacturing consistently at scale.
signal: ₹27.4 Cr seed; Ather's Tarun Mehta participated
why: Founder-backing from an EV founder is a useful customer-side signal; cell manufacturing is capital-heavy, so RDI debt matters here.

tech: Low-cost electrodes and electrolysers for green hydrogen
problem: Green hydrogen is too expensive, partly because electrolysers cost a lot
eli12: Green hydrogen is made by zapping water with electricity to split it into hydrogen and oxygen. The machine that does it, an electrolyser, is expensive. Newtrace makes cheaper electrodes, the parts where the splitting happens. The hard part is cheap and long-lasting at the same time.
signal: $6.3M pre-Series A led by HDFC Bank and Mitsui Sumitomo Insurance VC, to scale manufacturing
why: A bank leading a climate hardware round is unusual and signals project-finance appetite; entry may already be late for a seed investor.

tech: Magnetic confinement fusion
problem: Clean, always-on power without long-lived nuclear waste
eli12: The sun makes energy by squeezing tiny atoms together until they fuse. Pranos is trying to do that on Earth, holding super-hot gas in place with powerful magnets because no wall could survive touching it. If it works, it's nearly limitless clean power. It's one of the hardest engineering problems there is.
signal: $6.8M seed co-led by pi Ventures and Ankur Capital; Industrial47 backed the pre-seed
why: One of very few Indian magnetic-confinement efforts; the value is in milestone-gated capital, not near-term revenue.

tech: CRISPR platforms for diagnostics and gene editing
problem: Fast, cheap molecular tests and gene-editing tools are mostly imported
eli12: CRISPR is like a pair of molecular scissors with a search function: it finds one exact piece of DNA. CrisprBits uses the search part to make quick disease tests, and the scissors part for gene editing in health, food and farming. The hard part is getting tests accurate enough for doctors and approved by regulators.
signal: $3M pre-Series A led by Spectrum Impact
why: A platform with diagnostics revenue as the near-term path and gene editing as the option value.

tech: Synthetic biology and precision fermentation for food, nutrition and personal-care ingredients
problem: High-value ingredients depend on animal farming or imports
eli12: Precision fermentation is like brewing beer, but the yeast is reprogrammed to make a specific protein or ingredient instead of alcohol. StrainX engineers those microbes and builds the factories to brew at scale. The hard part is getting the cost per kilo low enough to beat the traditional way.
signal: $13M from Prime Venture Partners and Leo Capital as it exits stealth; scaling demo to commercial
why: India's cost advantage in biomanufacturing is real; this is a scale-up bet, likely past a seed investor's entry window.

tech: Bio-fertiliser made from waste, cutting chemical fertiliser use
problem: Farmers overuse chemical fertilisers, which hurts soil health and costs a lot
eli12: Plants need food from the soil. Cropcoin turns waste into a natural fertiliser full of helpful microbes, so farmers can use less chemical fertiliser. It's already selling, and is expanding from 10 to 66 districts.
signal: $1.5M pre-Series A led by Unicorn India Ventures with Climate Angels
why: Distribution-led agri-bio with revenue; the question is margin and repeatability, not science.

tech: AI-powered, portable brain-injury detection
problem: Head-injury patients often reach hospitals without CT scanners, losing critical time
eli12: After a bad knock to the head, doctors need to know fast if there's bleeding inside. That usually needs a big CT scanner many small hospitals don't have. Bioscan makes a portable device that screens for it in minutes, with AI helping read the result. The hard part is being accurate enough to trust in an emergency.
signal: $1M seed led by Unicorn India Ventures for market expansion
why: Triage at the ambulance or district hospital is a large unserved market; clinical evidence and reimbursement decide the outcome.

tech: AI-driven diagnostics for diabetic foot complications
problem: Diabetic foot ulcers are caught late and lead to avoidable amputations
eli12: People with diabetes can lose feeling in their feet, so a small wound goes unnoticed and gets serious. Ayati makes devices that check feet early, with AI spotting the warning signs before a wound appears. The hard part is getting busy clinics to use it on every patient.
signal: ₹15 Cr pre-Series A led by Inflexor Ventures; first institutional round
why: India's diabetes burden makes screening a volume business; the moat is clinical workflow, not the sensor.

tech: Re-engineered medical equipment manufacturing
problem: Hospital equipment is expensive and largely imported
eli12: Hospitals depend on machines that are mostly built abroad and cost a lot to buy and fix. Pulse wants to redesign how that equipment is made in India so it's cheaper. The source doesn't describe the exact devices yet, so this one needs a closer look.
signal: $4M seed led by 3one4 Capital with Incubate Fund Asia and Stride Ventures
why: Import substitution in hospital hardware is large, but the source is thin; needs primary research before scoring holds.

tech: Wearable photobiomodulation (light therapy) for pain
problem: Musculoskeletal pain is usually managed with drugs
eli12: Photobiomodulation means shining specific red and infrared light on sore muscles and joints to help them heal and hurt less. CURAPOD puts that light into a wearable pad. It's already sold directly to people and through gyms.
signal: ₹20 Cr pre-Series A; FDA-registered device, DTC and gym channels
why: Consumer-health distribution story more than deep science; outside the core of the thesis.

founders: Shashikant Singh Kunwar (co-founder & CTO); others not named
tech: Quantum-inspired software for complex planning, finance and defence/space data problems
problem: Some optimisation problems take normal computers far too long
eli12: Some puzzles, like planning thousands of delivery routes, have so many options a normal computer would take forever to check them all. Quantum-inspired methods borrow tricks from quantum physics to find good answers much faster, on ordinary computers. The hard part is proving it beats the best normal methods.
signal: ₹2 Cr raise; based at IIT Madras Research Park
why: Small, early and incubator-based, so closer to uncontested than most here, but 'quantum-inspired' needs hard benchmarks.

tech: Li-Fi: wireless data over light
problem: Radio Wi-Fi is crowded, and some sites (defence, hospitals) need interference-free links
eli12: Li-Fi is Wi-Fi using light instead of radio. An LED flickers on and off millions of times a second, too fast to see, and a sensor reads it like Morse code. It can't pass through walls, which is a feature for security. The hard part is getting it into real buildings at a price that makes sense.
signal: ₹30 Cr seed / pre-Series A
why: Niche secure-connectivity use cases fit; mass-market Li-Fi has a long history of disappointing, so focus on defence and industrial buyers.
